title: Tell me about a time you made a fast decision with incomplete information
prompt: Tell me about a time you had to decide what to do under time pressure without all the information you wanted. Explain how you weighed acting, checking, pausing or escalating, and what happened. A work, study, community or everyday responsibility can provide the example.
blurb: Bias for action: did they move decisively on limited info AND manage the risk — or just gamble?

rubric.label: Situation & time pressure
rubric.description: Explains a specific uncertain decision, the relevant time constraint and what information was missing.

rubric.label: Owning the call
rubric.description: Explains their responsibility and why acting, obtaining a quick check, pausing or escalating was appropriate within their authority.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Describes a concrete decision process: available evidence, assumptions, downside, reversibility and a proportionate check or safeguard.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes the observed outcome and limits of attribution using qualitative or quantitative evidence; a lucky result does not by itself validate the decision.

rubric.label: Reflection & calibration
rubric.description: Explains what would change the decision and how the stakes and reversibility affect the amount of checking needed.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore a decision made with limited information and a meaningful time constraint. The issue can arise in a shift, class, community activity or professional role. Assess calibration of speed, uncertainty and safety, not a preference for taking action in every case.
model_points: Clarifies the decision, missing information and cost or risk of waiting without inventing figures.
Identifies what was within their authority and when a responsible decision-maker needed to be involved.
Uses accessible evidence or a proportionate check before a reversible step, or explains why stopping was warranted.
Communicates a material assumption or risk to someone affected when appropriate.
Describes what actually happened, including unresolved effects, and separates decision quality from luck.
Explains a concrete change in future decision-making or what evidence would have justified another choice.

probes.trigger: candidate states a decision without its evidence
probes.question: What information did you use at that point?

probes.trigger: the proposed action may be outside their authority
probes.question: What was within your authority in that situation?

probes.trigger: candidate relies only on a successful outcome
probes.question: How would you judge the decision using only what you knew then?

red_flags: Acts despite an identified serious risk without a safeguard or a reasoned decision to proceed.
Presents an assumption as a verified observation after the distinction is clarified.
Takes credit for a decision made by someone else despite their own account.
follow_ups: What information would have changed your choice?
When would pausing or escalating have been the better decision?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. At a community event, rain threatened an outdoor activity. I checked the forecast and asked the organizer which indoor space was approved. We moved only the equipment that was safe to move and paused the outdoor setup. The activity started later but everyone could participate. I could not know whether the rain would worsen, so I chose an approved, reversible option and kept the organizer informed.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
